passage: I'm Sumit, and I'm in the same science project group as Mridul. Mridul has always said science is boring. He yawns in every lab. But when the four of us formed a group for the district science fair, he came to every meeting, even the Saturday ones. He stayed late to paint the volcano model, and he went to three shops to find baking soda. When our teacher asked him why he worked so hard, he shrugged and said, "Because it's us." I can't say he suddenly loves science; he still calls it boring. But when our group won second place, he held the certificate like it was gold.

qa.q: How many shops did Mridul go to for baking soda?
qa.a: He went to three shops to find baking soda.

qa.q: What does Mridul's 'Because it's us' reveal about why he worked so hard?
qa.a: It shows Mridul felt connected to the group; being part of his friends' team, not science, kept him coming every Saturday.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next term to keep Mridul this involved?
qa.a: The teacher could keep him in the same group for other projects, since belonging seems to power his effort.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit to see Mridul hold the certificate?
qa.a: Sumit sees how much the group means to Mridul, even though Mridul still calls science boring 🙂.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy who finds science boring work hard because the project group matters to him.

passage:
June: Pankaj sat alone at the back and did the minimum in English. His answers were half-lines. "I don't like English," he told his mother.
August: Uma asked him to join her reading circle, four kids who met at lunch to read one story aloud and act out a bit of it. Pankaj said yes because Uma and the others were fun, not because of the stories. He started practising his lines at home so he wouldn't let them down.
November: The circle had read eleven stories. Pankaj still said English was "okay only", but he had written a full page for the class magazine, because the circle was writing together.

qa.q: What did Uma's reading circle do at lunch?
qa.a: Four kids met to read one story aloud and act out a bit of it.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj start practising his lines at home?
qa.a: He didn't want to let Uma and the others down; the circle mattered to him more than the stories did.

qa.q: What choice by Uma made the difference for Pankaj?
qa.a: Inviting him into a small, friendly group gave him a reason to try, since belonging drove effort that English alone couldn't.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother see the change by November?
qa.a: She may be surprised to see the boy who said 'I don't like English' writing a full page for the class magazine.

grounding: Over months, a boy who dislikes English keeps working because a reading circle of friends matters to him.

passage: Ishita, you ask why I still keep this dusty quiz trophy? Let me tell you, your Pranav nana was no scholar. At eleven, I hated history. Dates, kings, all of it. But my three best friends, Kishore, Anwar and little Mani, decided to enter the inter-school quiz, and they wanted me. So every evening after school we sat on the temple steps with one borrowed book, quizzing each other till the lamps came on. I learned dates I never cared about, just so I wouldn't be the one who let them down. We came first. Mani cried. Honestly, I don't remember a single king now. But I remember those steps, the smell of the lamp oil, the four of us.

qa.q: Where did the four friends study every evening?
qa.a: On the temple steps, with one borrowed book, quizzing each other till the lamps came on.

qa.q: Why did Pranav learn dates he never cared about?
qa.a: He didn't want to be the one who let his three best friends down; the group, not history, kept him going.

qa.q: What could Ishita take from this story for a subject that feels dull?
qa.a: Ishita could join or form a small study group with friends, letting belonging supply the reason to keep going.

qa.q: Why might Mani have cried when they won?
qa.a: Mani probably felt overjoyed and proud of the whole group after all those evenings together on the steps.

grounding: A grandfather recalls studying history he disliked because his group of friends mattered to him.

passage:
Neelam had never cared about science. Plants, pulleys, whatever. But this term Swati had pulled her into the Sunflower Group with three other girls, and the group had a model of the water cycle due on Friday.
On Thursday evening the power went out in their whole colony. The glue gun died halfway through the clouds.
Neelam could have gone home. Instead she ran to her house for candles and a tube of craft glue, and stayed till nine, cutting cotton-wool clouds by candlelight while Swati read out the steps.
'You don't even like science,' Swati said, laughing.
'I like us,' Neelam said, and pressed the last cloud into place.
Years later Neelam would still remember the smell of wax and wet cotton, and the five of them lifting the model onto the teacher's table together.

qa.q: What did the Sunflower Group have to make?
qa.a: A model of the water cycle, due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Neelam stay till nine when she didn't care about science?
qa.a: The group mattered to her; being part of 'us' with Swati and the others made the work worth doing, power cut or not.

qa.q: What choice showed belonging at work, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Running home for candles and glue instead of leaving; the group finished the model and carried it up together on Friday.

qa.q: How might Swati feel hearing 'I like us'?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel warm and pleased, knowing that pulling Neelam into the group made her feel she belonged.

grounding: A child who does not care about the subject works hard on a group model through a power cut because the group matters to her.

passage:
Every Saturday at four, the colony community hall in Indore filled up for Maths Club: six kids, one whiteboard, a plate of Mrs Joshi's poha. Anmol had joined only because Rishabh begged him to.
'I hate maths,' Anmol said the first week.
But he kept coming. He liked the way Rishabh saved him a seat by the window. He liked their team name, the Zeros, and their silly handshake. When the Zeros had to solve twelve puzzles for the colony quiz, Anmol stayed back two extra Saturdays so he wouldn't be the one who let them down.
He still said he hated maths. But by December he was solving the logic puzzles faster than anyone, because the Zeros needed him to.

qa.q: What did the Maths Club call their team?
qa.a: The Zeros.

qa.q: Why did Anmol stay back two extra Saturdays?
qa.a: He didn't want to be the one who let the Zeros down; belonging to the group mattered more to him than the maths itself.

qa.q: Which of Rishabh's choices helped Anmol keep coming, and why?
qa.a: Begging him to join and saving him a seat by the window; feeling wanted in the group kept Anmol turning up and working.

qa.q: How might Rishabh see Anmol's 'I hate maths' by December?
qa.a: Rishabh probably finds it funny, since Anmol is now the fastest at logic puzzles, and knows the group is the real reason Anmol keeps coming.

grounding: A child who says he hates maths keeps going to a maths club and works hard because the group and his friend matter to him.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, February.
Amandeep has never cared much for science. He does the minimum and forgets it. This month, four boys from his row started meeting at lunch to prepare for the inter-school science quiz, and Amandeep joined them, I think mainly because his best friends were there. The change has been striking. He comes early to sit with them. He made flashcards of the planets because the group needed someone to do it. On Tuesday he stayed back to ask me about Saturn's rings so he wouldn't 'let the team down'. He still says science is boring. But he hasn't missed one lunch meeting. Next step: I'll keep the group together for next term's project and give Amandeep a named role, so the belonging that keeps him coming stays strong.
Jyoti

qa.q: What did Amandeep make for the group?
qa.a: He made flashcards of the planets.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep ask about Saturn's rings?
qa.a: He cared about his friends and didn't want to let the team down, so belonging made him keen to learn even though he finds science boring.

qa.q: What step does the teacher plan, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the group together and giving Amandeep a named role, so the belonging that keeps him working stays strong.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's friends see him now?
qa.a: They probably see him as a real part of the team, relying on his flashcards.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who dislikes science working hard because his friends' quiz group matters to him.

passage:
Wednesday
Today was the third study-group day at Tushar's house. Five of us round his dining table doing olympiad sums, and his mother made poha. I don't even like maths that much. But I like the group. I like when Tushar groans and everyone laughs. I like that when I finally got the triangle question, everyone clapped as if I'd scored a goal.
I did two extra pages at home tonight so I don't slow them down on Friday. Mummy asked why I'm suddenly doing maths without being told. I said, because the others will ask me.
It reminds me of last year's craft club, when we all stayed late making the paper boat for the fair. I miss that. Maybe this can be like that.
Nikita

qa.q: What did Tushar's mother make?
qa.a: She made poha.

qa.q: Why did Nikita do two extra pages at home?
qa.a: Nikita cares about the group and feels happy and included there, so not slowing them down matters more than maths itself.

qa.q: How could a teacher use what Nikita's diary shows?
qa.a: By keeping friendly study groups going, since belonging can keep children working even at subjects they don't love.

qa.q: How might the others in the group feel when Nikita solves the triangle question?
qa.a: They seem pleased and celebratory, clapping as if Nikita had scored a goal.

grounding: A child's diary shows extra maths work done not for the subject but because the friends' study group matters.

passage: In Dhamtari, the children of the lower lane gathered every evening under the big neem tree near the panchayat hall, where Hemant's elder sister helped them with homework by lantern light. Pankaj had never cared for homework. But Hemant was his best friend, and all his friends were under that tree. So he started going. At first he just sat there. Then Hemant's sister gave each of them a job: Pankaj held the lantern and checked everyone's tables. He learnt the tables himself so he could check them properly. By the end of the month he could say the seven-times table faster than anyone. 'You like maths now?' Hemant asked. Pankaj shrugged. 'I like the neem tree,' he said, and everyone laughed.

qa.q: Where did the children gather every evening?
qa.a: They gathered under the big neem tree near the panchayat hall.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj start going to the study circle?
qa.a: He wanted to be with Hemant and his friends and would have felt left out otherwise, so the pull of belonging, not homework, brought him there.

qa.q: What did Hemant's sister do that turned belonging into learning?
qa.a: She gave Pankaj a real job, holding the lantern and checking tables, which made him learn the tables himself.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel when Pankaj says 'I like the neem tree'?
qa.a: Hemant would likely feel amused and happy that his friend enjoys being part of the group.

grounding: A village child who never cared for homework joins an evening study circle because his friends are there, and learns his tables.

passage:
Bilal didn't care about geography. Rivers, rainfall, capital cities: boring.
But at his new school in Johannesburg, Zanele and three others met every Tuesday in the library corner to do homework together. They laughed, shared crisps and called themselves “the Corner.”
Zanele waved him over in his second week. “You can join the Corner if you want.”
So Bilal came every Tuesday. He did his geography because they were doing geography. When he got a map wrong, Zanele showed him. When he got one right, Themba high-fived him.
By the end of term his geography mark had gone up a whole grade. His mother asked what happened.
“I just didn't want to miss Tuesdays,” he said. He still thought rivers were boring. He just liked the Corner.

qa.q: On which day did the Corner meet?
qa.a: They met every Tuesday in the library corner.

qa.q: Why did Bilal keep doing geography even though he found it boring?
qa.a: He felt included and happy in the Corner, and didn't want to miss being part of the group.

qa.q: What could Bilal's mother do to support what is working?
qa.a: Make sure he can keep going on Tuesdays and ask him about the group, since belonging is keeping him going.

qa.q: How might Zanele feel knowing Bilal kept coming?
qa.a: Zanele might feel pleased and proud that inviting the new boy made him feel he belonged.

grounding: The passage shows a child working at a subject he finds boring because a study group matters to him.

passage:
At the boarding school in Kalimpong, the Class 6 girls in Dorm 3 had a study circle every evening after dinner, on the floor between the beds.
Dolma hated science. But Afreen and the others sat in the circle every night, notebooks open, whispering answers, sharing a torch when the lights dimmed.
The first week, Dolma sat on her bed and pretended to read. The second week, Afreen patted the floor. “Come. We saved you a spot.”
Dolma came. She opened her science book because everyone else had theirs open. She asked a question. Afreen explained it with her hands.
By the end of the month Dolma was doing her science homework every night, without fail. When the matron asked if she'd started liking science, Dolma thought about it. “No,” she said. “I like the circle.”

qa.q: Where did the study circle meet?
qa.a: They met on the floor between the beds in Dorm 3 every evening after dinner.

qa.q: Why did Dolma start doing science homework every night?
qa.a: She felt welcomed and happy in the circle; belonging mattered more to her than the subject.

qa.q: What could the matron do to support what is working?
qa.a: Protect the study-circle time and make sure every girl feels invited, since belonging keeps them going.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Dolma joining the circle?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels pleased and kind, glad to have made Dolma feel included.

grounding: The passage shows a child doing homework in a subject she dislikes because she belongs to a study circle.

passage:
Before: In the summer holidays, Vaibhav didn't open a book. Maths was dull, and he was always the last to finish.
During: In July, his friend Anand started a “maths gang” with four boys after school, under the neem tree by the gate. Vaibhav joined for the company. They argued over sums, made up silly names for the numbers, and shared sugar-cane juice. Vaibhav started doing his worksheets just to keep up with them.
After: In December, Anand's family moved to Nashik and the maths gang stopped. Vaibhav sat alone under the neem tree one afternoon with a worksheet, and felt a tug of missing them. He still didn't love maths. But he did the worksheet anyway, thinking of the gang, and got every sum right.

qa.q: Where did the maths gang meet?
qa.a: They met after school under the neem tree by the gate.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel under the neem tree in December?
qa.a: He felt a nostalgic tug of missing the gang, and the memory of belonging still pushed him to finish the worksheet.

qa.q: What could help Vaibhav keep going now the gang has stopped?
qa.a: He could start a new small study group with classmates, since belonging is what keeps him working.

qa.q: How might Anand feel if he knew Vaibhav still did his worksheets?
qa.a: Anand might feel happy and a little homesick, knowing his gang still mattered.

grounding: The three beats show a child doing maths because of a group of friends, with belonging keeping him going even after it ends.

passage: Raghav, you ask why I studied so hard as a boy when I didn't even like history? Let your Lokesh Thatha tell you. The summer I was eleven, four of us boys made a study group under the big banyan tree near the tank. Murali, Siva, Kannan and me. We met at three every afternoon. The others loved history. I didn't. But I loved them. I loved the jokes and the way Murali drew maps in the mud. So I read every chapter, just so I'd have something to say at three o'clock. By the end of that summer I knew more history than I ever thought I would. Not because of the kings and battles. Because of that banyan tree, and those three boys. I still think of them.

qa.q: Where did the four boys meet for their study group?
qa.a: Under the big banyan tree near the tank.

qa.q: Why did young Lokesh read every chapter even though he didn't like history?
qa.a: Young Lokesh loved his friends and wanted to belong, so reading every chapter gave him something to say at the group.

qa.q: What choice in the story kept Lokesh studying all summer?
qa.a: Joining the study group under the banyan tree, where belonging gave young Lokesh a reason to keep reading.

qa.q: How might Murali and the others have felt about Lokesh joining them?
qa.a: They probably felt glad to have him, enjoying his company and his effort to join the talk.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a summer study group where he worked hard at a subject he didn't love, because the group mattered to him.

passage: It was the week before the Christmas holidays, and Ishita's class had formed a "science squad" of four to make a volcano model. Ishita didn't care about volcanoes. But Chetan, Meher and Arun were her favourite people in class, and the squad had a secret handshake. On the last evening before the model was due, the power went out in her building. The others were at Chetan's house. Ishita could have stayed home. Instead she took her torch and walked two lanes over. By candlelight, she mixed the baking soda paste, measured, and fixed the crooked cone three times. Chetan said, "You're the most careful one." Ishita blushed. She still didn't love volcanoes. But she'd never worked so hard on anything, because the squad was counting on her.

qa.q: How many times did Ishita fix the crooked cone?
qa.a: She fixed the crooked cone three times.

qa.q: Why did Ishita work so hard on a subject she didn't care about?
qa.a: She loved being part of the squad and felt she belonged, so she worked hard because the group was counting on her.

qa.q: What does Ishita's walk through the dark show about belonging?
qa.a: That wanting to be with the group gave her the persistence to keep going even when it was hard.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about Ishita's care with the model?
qa.a: Chetan seemed impressed and grateful, calling her the most careful one.

grounding: Before Christmas a girl who doesn't love science works hard on a group model through a power cut because the group matters to her.

passage: During Gurpurab week, Gurleen's class in Ludhiana formed maths groups for the inter-school quiz. Gurleen found maths boring. But her best friend Manjula joined the "Number Ninjas", so Gurleen did too. The Ninjas met at lunch every day in the corner of the playground, sharing parathas and doing practice sums. Gurleen wanted to keep up, so at home she practised tables in the bath. Her mother was astonished. "You're doing maths by yourself?" "The Ninjas need me," Gurleen said. At the quiz, she answered the question on fractions and the whole team cheered. She grinned. She still didn't love maths, exactly. But she loved the Ninjas, and that was enough to make her work.

qa.q: Where did the Number Ninjas meet at lunch?
qa.a: In the corner of the playground.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen practise tables in the bath even though maths bored her?
qa.a: She wanted to belong and keep up with Manjula and the Ninjas, so the group gave her a reason to work.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's story show about belonging?
qa.a: That wanting to be part of a group can keep a child working hard even at a subject she doesn't enjoy.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's mother feel seeing her do maths alone?
qa.a: Her mother was astonished and probably delighted.

grounding: During Gurpurab week a girl who finds maths boring joins a maths group because of her friend and works hard because the group matters.

passage:
"Aadhya, it's the Christmas holidays. Why are you doing science at nine at night?"
"It's for the group, Amma! Me, Mitali, Rhea and Joel. We're making the solar system."
"You told me science is the most boring subject in the world."
"It is. Planets are boring."
"Then why are you painting Saturn for the third time?"
"Because Joel said my first Saturn looked like an egg. And Rhea's Jupiter is so nice, I can't be the one with the bad planet. We're the Space Cadets. We present on Monday."
"And if it were just you?"
"Then I'd do it on Sunday night and cry." Aadhya dipped the brush again. "But they're waiting for my Saturn."
Aparna laughed and brought her a cup of milk.

qa.q: Which planet is Aadhya painting for the third time?
qa.a: Saturn.

qa.q: Why does Aadhya keep working on a subject she finds boring?
qa.a: Aadhya feels part of the Space Cadets and doesn't want to let them down; that sense of belonging, not the planets, makes her eager to keep going.

qa.q: How could a teacher use what works for Aadhya?
qa.a: Keep giving her group projects where friends depend on each other, so belonging carries her through subjects she doesn't love yet.

qa.q: How might Aparna see her daughter's late-night painting?
qa.a: Aparna seems amused and a little surprised that "the most boring subject" is getting three Saturns, and can see the group matters more than the subject.

grounding: A child works late on a science project she finds boring because her group matters to her, showing belonging as an engine of effort.
